chapters.title: Two trees
narration: It will take me 2 whole pine trees to harvest all of the wood a 300 square foot house needs. No lumber yard and no delivery truck, just the trees already standing on the property, and one small chainsaw.

chapters.title: The fell line
narration: It starts with a notch, cut into the side I want it to fall toward, and then a back cut from the other side, a little higher. The strip of wood left between the two is the hinge. It steers the tree all the way over, and it is why felling gets a chapter of its own before any of this is safe to try. The saw is a 38.2 cc hardware-store model with a 16 inch bar.

chapters.title: All at once
narration: Then everything happens at once. The crown comes off, the trunk is cut into 8 sections, 6 feet each, and every section splits into 8 wedges. That is 64 struts from one tree. With 2 trees it is 128, for a frame that needs 120.

chapters.title: Why split it
narration: Why split it instead of milling it square? Because the only wood a split loses is the width of the cut. Of the 318 board feet in this trunk, the saw takes 40 and the wedges keep 278, which is 87.4 percent of the tree standing in the frame. The honest cost is the stick itself. From a small log, a single wedge is the weaker stick in bending, and it is the triangulated shell, not the wedge, that makes it enough.

chapters.title: Measured, and guessed
narration: Before the days and the fuel, here is what those figures rest on. The fuel rate was measured, in one timed sitting with the tanks counted. The ripping hours come from the cutting rate, which was also measured. The day plan is a decision, not a result. And the size of the saw's tank is an estimate, because the listings disagree and nobody has checked this saw, so the fuel comes out as a range.

chapters.title: What it took
narration: The whole harvest takes 8 days: 2 of felling, 2 of bucking, and 4 of ripping. Ripping is the part that was timed with the fuel written down: 2 tanks an hour, for 24 hours. That is 48 tanks, and at 0.28 to 0.37 litres a tank, somewhere between 3.6 and 4.7 US gallons. Felling and bucking were never metered, so they are not in that number.

chapters.title: What the house numbers rest on
narration: Now the question every build gets asked: what is it worth? Before a single house figure, here is what they rest on. The published ones come from the home builders' association's cost survey, the Census Bureau and the Bureau of Labor Statistics, and the builders' survey is a small one, which its own authors say. The 200,000 dollar house, the 100,000 dollar trailer, the 40 percent labor share and the 80 hours of shell work are my own round figures. The tax bracket is a decision. Everything else is an estimate, and it is labelled as one.

chapters.title: Where a house's time goes
narration: A new house takes 7.6 months on average, from the first shovel to finished, by the Census Bureau's count, and 15.1 months when its owner builds it. One builder's week by week schedule shows where that time goes. 15 percent is the ground and the foundation. 10 percent is framing. 7.5 percent is pipes, wires and ducts. 27.5 percent is the inside: insulation, drywall, floors, trim, paint and fixtures. 10 percent is the outside, 15 percent the driveway, yard and clean up, and the last 15 percent is inspection and closing.

chapters.title: Where a house's money goes
narration: Now the money, in the shares the builders' survey found. Of a 200,000 dollar new house, 27,400 dollars is the land. 128,700 is the building itself. 33,400 is the builder's overhead and profit, and 10,500 is the commission, marketing and financing it takes to sell it. At the survey's national average, that much new house is only about 796 square feet.

chapters.title: Labor is not most of it
narration: So is labor most of what you pay for? Not in a new house. Take my 40 percent of the building as labor, and it is 25.7 percent of the price. Then put the lumber at its record. In the spring of twenty twenty one, framing lumber topped 1,500 dollars a thousand board feet, and the builders worked out it added 35,872 dollars to an average new home. Price this house that way and it comes to 214,800: 82,200 in materials, 51,500 in labor, 9,800 in permits, fees and design, 27,400 for the land, 33,400 to the builder and 10,500 to sell it. Labor is 24 percent. About a quarter.

chapters.title: The trailer is built the other way
narration: A new manufactured home splits another way. Of a 100,000 dollar home, about 20,000 is the dealer's share. 46,000 is what the factory spends on materials, 16,800 is its payroll, and 17,200 is its overhead and profit. Factory labor is only 16.8 percent of the price. At the Census average of 86.62 dollars a square foot, that buys about 1,154 square feet, set up, without the land. The factory split is from the two thousand two Economic Census, the newest published in that detail, so read it as a shape more than a figure.

chapters.title: What the fortnight is worth
narration: Now the frame this film has been building. Framing is 16.6 percent of what it costs to build a new house, which is 10.7 percent of its price. For 300 square feet, bought at the national rate with the builder's share, the frame costs 9,798 dollars. The fortnight spends 497 dollars: the saw, the fuel, the hardware, and the two trees at what a timber buyer would pay for them standing. That keeps 9,301 dollars, for 80 hours of hands-on work. 116 dollars an hour. Against a manufactured home's cheaper rate it is 59. A carpenter's median wage is 29.12 an hour, and a typical worker takes home 19.69, so buying that frame would cost 498 hours of ordinary pay.

chapters.title: Every part of the house
narration: Here is every part of the house, done the same way for 300 square feet: what it costs to buy, what the dome way still pays in money, and how many hours of a typical worker's take-home pay the difference is worth. Fees stay fees. The foundation is shorter, because a circle has the least edge for its floor. The skin is smaller but harder to finish, and the pipes and wires run from a central column instead of around the walls. The last line is the whole floor, if every hour of the work is yours.

chapters.title: Where the saving comes from
narration: Stack it all up and the saving has four sources. Bought whole, the floor costs 65,100 dollars. 16,600 of that is the builder's and the seller's share, which anyone who builds their own house keeps, whatever its shape. 17,300 is labor you do yourself, paid in hours instead of money. 3,200 is lumber from your own trees instead of a yard. And 4,300 is the shape itself: 55 percent less framing, 40 percent less skin, a 12 percent shorter foundation, and runs 44 percent shorter from the central column. That leaves 23,700 dollars to pay.

chapters.title: What this does not show
narration: And what it does not show. 37 percent of what a house costs to build does not care about its shape: fees, windows, cabinets, appliances, floors, the driveway. Only the frame's hours were measured; the rest of that labor is weeks more of somebody's time, and wiring, plumbing and gas usually need a licensed trade and an inspection. A triangle is harder to finish than a flat wall, and the dome's laminate skin is its most expensive material. Against a manufactured home the gap is small: 300 square feet at a trailer's average price is 25,986 dollars, and the dome way pays 16,444 for the same parts, before your hours. And the biggest saving here, the builder's share and the labor, belongs to anyone who builds their own house, whatever its shape.

chapters.title: Do the one thing
narration: If any of this was worth your time, send it to one person who can
carry it further than I can. That is the whole ask. One share from
somebody with reach does more for this than a month of me in a field
with a chainsaw.
